title: AI Cheating as a Failure to Love
author: Alan Noble
summary: Alan Noble argues that the root cause of rampant AI cheating in higher education is not technological but moral: a lack of the virtue of love. Contemporary students approach college with an efficiency mindset -- completing tasks as quickly as possible for GPA and career credentials -- rather than a love of wisdom. Noble contends that when students truly love a subject, the allure of AI as an efficiency tool loses its grip. Teachers can cultivate this love by modeling their own passion for their subjects, inviting students into genuine inquiry. Insofar as education is organized around Jacques Ellul's 'technique' (maximal efficiency), students rationally gravitate toward the most efficient tool available. The solution is not technological banning or surrender but pedagogical: teaching students to love what is lovely in each discipline, understanding knowledge as worthy of pursuit for its own sake.
points: * Students' AI misuse reflects a deeper orientation toward education as task-completion rather than the pursuit of wisdom -- they have been conditioned to equate worth with GPA and credentials. * Contemporary pressures (high tuition, anxious credentialism, GPA-as-identity) reinforce the efficiency mindset that makes AI cheating seem rational and even responsible. * Teachers who embody their love for a subject can model 'what loving wisdom looks and feels like' -- Janetos observed students 'catching the passion' when teachers showed genuine excitement. * Ellul's 'technique' -- maximal efficiency as the organizing principle -- explains why AI becomes irresistible in a school culture that rewards performance over wisdom. * Noble: 'The challenge before administrators and educators is less, How can we catch AI cheaters? but, How have we been subtly reinforcing maximal efficiency instead of the virtue of love?' * Some students will refuse the invitation to love; teachers cannot force it, but their vocation is to keep putting the invitation before students.
quotes: What if at the root of students' misuse of AI to avoid studying is a fundamental lack of love?

Insofar as contemporary education is motivated by a drive for maximal efficiency, what Jacques Ellul calls technique, rather than love of wisdom and knowledge, students will naturally and quite reasonably gravitate towards tools that are the pinnacle of efficiency.

When a teacher makes a compelling case for why students should love a subject, students are invited to seek the wisdom in that subject out of passion, out of a desire in their hearts and minds, rather than out of a drive to efficiently pass the course.
Your task as a teacher is to always put before them the invitation to come home, to see the grandeur of God's world and to explore it earnestly with all of their strength and all of their mind.
The challenge before administrators and educators is less, 'How can we catch AI cheaters?' but, 'How have we been subtly reinforcing maximal efficiency instead of the virtue of love?'
